newsitem.title: GERMANY: Congressman slams Bonn museum's portrayal of Jews.
newsitem.headline: Congressman slams Bonn museum's portrayal of Jews.

text.p: A senior member of the U.S. Congress slammed Germany's flagship history museum on Wednesday, accusing it of portraying Jews as "sub-human" and saying it was absurd that its permanent exhibition depicted little before 1945.

Tom Lantos, a Jewish California Democrat who came to the United States after surviving the Holocaust in Nazi-occupied Hungary, said the Museum of Contemporary History in Bonn did not devote nearly enough space to German Jews and their fate.

"There's a small room... which deals with the Holocaust and then 4,000 square metres dealing with economic and social development since 1945," said Lantos, a member of the House of Representatives' International Relations Committee.
"That's very interesting but that's like taking O.J. Simpson and having him discuss his golf game, rather than the seminal event in his life," Lantos told a news briefing.

German journalists pointed out to the congressman that the brief of the museum -- a pet project of Chancellor Helmut Kohl -- was post-war history, and a museum offering a comprehensive look at all German history was being built in Berlin.

"That is the absurdity of the museum," he responded. "This is like discussing the history of the blacks in the United States and beginning with the Emancipation Proclamation or discussing the history of South Africa beginning with the election of Mandela to the presidency."
He also lambasted the museum for not highlighting the contribution Jews made to every aspect of German life.

"It portrays Jews as sub-human in a Holocaust context rather than showing Jews for having been major contributors to German culture, history, civilisation, literature, music, art -- you name it," said Lantos, who toured the museum on Tuesday.

A spokeswoman for the museum said she was "shocked" at Lantos's criticism, adding the museum took great care to point up the links between Germany's past and present and had won international recognition for its work.
Kohl, a history graduate, proposed the museum's construction in his maiden speech as chancellor in 1982. The glass-fronted building stands just across the road from his chancellery.
Lantos said he had not raised the subject during talks with Kohl on Tuesday as their time was very limited but he hoped the chancellor would read his comments when they were published.
"The young generation in Germany desperately needs a candid look at history but this does anything but that," he said.
International Relations Committee chairman Benjamin Gilman, who is also Jewish, distanced himself from the tough criticism.
"I think we have to remind ourselves what the objectives of this museum were about," the New York Republican said.

"It wasn't intended to go before the period of 1945 and while we would have liked to have seen more emphasis on that aspect, I think we do have to recognise that it was intended to depict German progress from '45 to the present time."
Lantos singled out one picture at the museum, showing a Soviet soldier taking away a German woman's bicycle, as typical of its portrayal of history.
"What was not shown was the 20 million Soviet citizens who were killed because of Hitler's war on the Soviet Union," he said.
